correctness.rationale: All successful initial sets are partitioned exhaustively by the number of core-bearing parts (0, 1 or at least 2). The first-forcing obstructions give necessary and sufficient vacancy conditions; algebraic weight enumeration over the four core--leaf states produces the formula with no overcount. Boundary assumptions r>=2 and n_i>=2 are used in the two-vacancy different-part case. An independently coded brute-force propagation and coefficient checker produced zero mismatches over 156,928 subsets in seven independent multipartite profiles, while the general combinatorial proof handles arbitrary admissible sizes. The 2-sensor count follows from an exhaustive classification of weight-two feasible sets; no claim that experiments prove the infinite theorem.

originality.rationale: The primary initiating source explicitly left the leaf-corona polynomial for arbitrary bases open (Question 3); its own formula addresses clique attachment size strictly greater than one. The new iff profile and closed polynomial settle the question on multipartite bases having at least two vertices in every part. The 2023 reliability transform changes variables but does not produce this base-family polynomial. Semantic searches in published records did not return a covering theorem. Residual unindexed equivalences remain possible.
residual_risks: An independently published, unpublished or unindexed equivalent all-subset corona enumeration could evade the sources searched.
Published summaries of nearby results were not a substitute for reading their entire manuscripts; they appear conceptually distinct on the record, but implicit reductions could remain.
The theorem excludes singleton parts and arbitrary base graphs, and thus is a restricted answer to the original general question.

value.rationale: The original 2018 power-domination polynomial paper explicitly isolates the corona by a single leaf as an unresolved computational graph-family operation. A closed all-cardinality formula for an infinite, natural complete multipartite subclass goes materially beyond a minimum-value substitution: it identifies every admissible sensor subset and counts all initial placement sizes, which in turn gives exact full-observation failure reliability and precise multiplicity of optimal two-sensor placements. The exact number depends nontrivially on multipartite part sizes and includes forced-versus-deadlocked cases absent from a routine count.
